transcript:
Meeting header:
Date: 2026-10-29
Start: 16:00 UTC
Duration: 52 minutes
Attendees: Morgan Ellis (Redwood AE), Priya Nambiar (Redwood SE), Liam Chen (Redwood CSM); Sofia Ramirez (VP Eng, Vanguard Retail), Daniel Lowe (Platform SRE), Khalid Ahmed (Security), Maya Patel (Product)

Summary: quick discovery focused on reliability, incident tolerance, multi-region fallbacks, and SLA expectations. Customer is evaluating Hosted vs Dedicated vs Private for a checkout recommendation service. They care about multi-region failover, model fallback strategies, and auditability.

Topics: reliability requirements, expected outage scenarios, fallback policy design, SLA and metrics, security/compliance prerequisites, next steps and pilot scope.

Transcript:
[00:00] Morgan (Redwood): hey everyone, thanks for joining, i'm Morgan from Redwood, i'll kick off, we also have Priya our solutions engineer and Liam on CSM. how's everyone doing?
[00:14] Sofia (Vanguard): good, thanks. we ran a quick schedule check, 52 minutes sounds right.
[00:20] Morgan: awesome. quick agenda, we want to understand your reliability needs around the checkout recommender, especially incident tolerance, multi-region fallbacks, and then surface what Hosted vs Dedicated vs Private would look like operationally.
[00:32] Maya: yeah that's the main ask. our checkout recommender is customer facing and has to handle 800 rps peak, p99 strict, and we need a clear SLA if something goes wrong.
[00:45] Daniel: to add, we have strong constraints on PII not leaving certain regions and we already run a multi-region deployment for core services. thoughts on cross-region latency are important.
[00:56] Priya (Redwood SE): understood. can you talk through current infra -- are you routing requests via edge LB or through internal api gateway? and do you have existing model endpoints today?
[01:08] Sofia: it's via our api-gateway, we have an internal model infra but it's fairly batchy. for real-time recommender we want sub 200ms p95, p99 budget is tight.
[01:20] Morgan: perfect. just to calibrate, typical patterns we've seen: Hosted for fast time-to-value but with regional routing and fallback policies, Dedicated when you want predictable capacity and isolation, and Private when you need full network control or specific compliance. can i ask what would push you to Private vs Dedicated?
[01:38] Khalid (Security): for us, Private is attractive if we need explicit control over KMS keys and physical separation. also audit logging retention longer than our standard defaults.
[01:47] Maya: and the timeline, actually - we have a holiday ramp in december so we need a pilot by mid november ideally.
[01:56] Priya: ok got it. on incident scenarios, do you mean region failover (e.g., whole AZ/regional outage) or model performance degradation (higher latency or quality drift)?
[02:08] Daniel: both. we care about full-region failover and also degraded model performance. if a heavy request spike makes p99 jump, we want to be able to automatically fallback to a cheaper/faster variant.
[02:20] Priya: we support several fallback strategies: 1) model variant fallback - route to a smaller quantized model variant automatically if latency threshold breached, 2) region fallback - route to another region based on routing policy with health checks and active/passive or active-active options, 3) capacity tier fallback - move to hosted burst capacity or queued mode with degraded responses. these can be combined with circuit breakers and per-route SLOs.
[02:46] Sofia: hmm, how transparent is that for monitoring? we need token-level cost, latency per model, and tracing into our APM.
[02:55] Priya: we export per-route metrics, token and latency breakdowns, and there's integration with common tracing systems. note the auto-transcript sometimes garbles - we do send logs to your SIEM and you get per-request IDs.
[03:10] Daniel: important: how long does failover take for region fallback? we can't assume instant.
[03:16] Priya: it depends on DNS TTL, LB failover, and session affinity. with our recommended setup (active-active multi-region + smart routing), failover can be sub-second for new requests because routing happens at our edge and your gateway. for sticky sessions you might need session replication; otherwise there's a small cold-start for KV cache.
[03:34] Daniel: KV cache? we rely on KV cache for embeddings / context, if that's lost p99 will spike.
[03:40] Morgan: yeah that's a big one -- we have prefix/KV caching with fallback strategies: warm-up requests, progressive degradation where we serve truncated context, or fall back to a stateless smaller model to keep latency bounded. sometimes transcriptions show K V cash instead of cache, haha.
[03:53] Khalid: from security perspective, what's the pattern for key management and auditability when using Hosted? who holds KMS?
[04:00] Priya: Hosted uses Redwood-managed keys by default, but we support customer-managed KMS for Dedicated and Private, and in Hosted we also offer Bring-Your-Own-Key (BYOK) in certain enterprise plans. all events are logged and we can ship audit logs, we also support HSM integrations for Private.
[04:16] Khalid: okay can you share SOC 2 doc and KMS architecture?
[04:19] Priya: yes, i'll attach the security pack after call.
[04:22] Sofia: about SLA numbers, what do you typically guarantee? we read 99.9% for hosted, is there an option for higher?
[04:30] Morgan: standard Hosted SLA is 99.9% availability on request-level for production plans. Dedicated has stronger SLAs (99.95 or 99.99 depending on commit and configuration) because of reserved capacity and redundancy. Private SLAs are contractual and depend on the customer's infra and support tier.
[04:48] Maya: what's the SLO breakdown for latency vs availability? we need p99 latency not availability only.
[04:55] Priya: SLAs are typically availability based, but we provide SLO dashboards where you can set latency SLOs like p95/p99 and we can alert/regress rollouts if models breach them. for committed Dedicated customers we can negotiate latency-backed SLAs.
[05:10] Daniel: interesting, so for the spike scenario, we'd like an automatic model fallback but also a way to prefer correctness vs latency. can we set per-route policies?
[05:19] Priya: yes you can set policy sets per route: latency-first, quality-first, cost-first. each policy can specify thresholds (e.g., if p99 > 350ms for 3 consecutive mins then fallback to variant-x) and an automatic rollback window.
[05:34] Sofia: does fallback change the model's output shape or schema? our frontend expects consistent JSON.
[05:40] Morgan: good point. we support structured outputs and schema validation; you can pipeline a post-processor to normalize outputs. also we recommend model family fallbacks that are schema-compatible. sometimes transcription mislabels model names but the underlying runtime ensures compatible outputs if you pin the model set.
[05:58] Maya: on multi-region routing, are we looking at active-active or active-passive? we prefer active-active but worry about consistency for session data.
[06:07] Priya: active-active works well if you replicate the KV cache or are okay with eventual consistency. for strict consistency we recommend active-passive with quick failover plus session replication, or use sticky session with global cache sync. for checkout we typically recommend stateless requests where the session context is passed in the request to avoid cross-region KV replication complexity.
[06:30] Daniel: is there any observable where routing chooses region based on cost versus latency? we have cost-sensitive markets.
[06:36] Morgan: yeah routing policies can include cost tiers; you can prefer lower-cost region unless latency targets breached. there is also a circuit-breaker to avoid routing to regions with degraded performance.
[06:50] Khalid: one more on compliance: data residency - can Hosted pin data regionally? we have EU-only PII for certain users.
[06:59] Priya: yes, Hosted has regional isolation where requests and logs stay in region for a tenant, and Dedicated allows strict tenancy in specific regions. Private gives you full control. we'll share our data residency matrix.
[07:10] Maya: ok timing again - pilot mid november. what would pilot look like?
[07:16] Liam (CSM): typically a 2-week pilot: we provision dedicated test capacity or hosted tenant, set up routing for 2 regions, configure model variants and fallback policy, run load tests and sample traffic, and collect metrics. we provide runbook and ops support.
[07:30] Sofia: can we run our own p99 bench with our dataset?
[07:33] Priya: absolutely -- we'll give a bench harness and you can run it or we can run it with your spike dataset.
[07:39] Daniel: what about cost under fallback? if we route to region B or to a beefy model variant, how do we track and predict cost?
[07:46] Morgan: we give token-level cost breakdown, and for Dedicated we can show expected unit cost with reserved capacity math; for Hosted we provide historical cost estimates given traffic patterns and fallback scenarios. we'll include worst-case delta in the TCO spreadsheet.
[08:00] Maya: what's the expected work for our infra team to onboard? how much networking config?
[08:06] Priya: for Hosted it's minimal: API keys, VPC peering optional, and SSO. Dedicated requires VPC setup and private link, and Private requires full infra provisioning with our deployment package. we'll provide a checklist.
[08:19] Khalid: SSO and RBAC - do you integrate with our IdP and support scoped roles?
[08:24] Morgan: yes SSO via SAML/OIDC, SCIM for provisioning, and RBAC with per-route permissions.
[08:30] Sofia: any customer references for multi-region production?
[08:33] Morgan: we have customers in retail and payments running active-active multi-region setups; we'll share a short case study. sometimes the auto-transcript names get a bit off but the details are solid.
[08:44] Maya: ok let's recap and call out open items.
[08:48] Morgan: recap: we will send TCO/pricing, security pack, schedule technical deep dive and run pilot. open items: Daniel to share p99 targets and dataset, Morgan/Priya to share docs, Liam to set pilot workspace.
[08:58] Sofia: yep that works. any final Qs?
[09:01] Daniel: just one, for model fallback do you support gradual traffic shifting and canarying?
[09:06] Priya: yes, we support canary rollouts, traffic shifting percentages, and automatic rollback if SLOs breach.
[09:12] Khalid: good. thanks.
[09:14] Morgan: thanks everyone, we'll follow up with items and a calendar invite for the deep dive.
[09:20] [meeting ends]

Notes: transcript includes occasional mis-transcriptions typical of automated captions (e.g., K V cash/K V cache, V P C). the call was AE+SE led and included security and infra stakeholders.
